summary: Provides a framework for operating and managing Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks. It describes the significant technical issues for management solutions but leaves specific approaches, models and protocols out of scope. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4176 is a framework for running and managing Layer 3 VPNs, which are the private networks a provider builds across a shared backbone. It describes what the customer-facing management has to do, what the provider's own network management has to do, and how the two are related. It stops short of saying how any of it should be implemented.

subtitle: What has to be managed when a provider runs Layer 3 VPNs for its customers.

tldr.problem: A provider that sells Layer 3 VPNs has to answer two different sets of questions: what the customer wants to see and change, and what the provider has to build and keep running, and nobody had written down how those two fit together.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out a reference model with three management layers, two management functions, the five traditional management categories, and the pieces of an L3VPN that each of them covers.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that deliberately chooses no protocol and no information model. The selection of specific approaches, and choices among information models and protocols, are stated to be outside its scope.

facts.value: Y. El Mghazli and T. Nadeau

facts.value: 5, fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security

today: RFC 4176 is an Informational memo published in October 2005, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It provides a framework for L3VPN operations and management, and states that the choice of specific approaches, information models and protocols is left to other work.

sections.title: What the Framework Covers
sections.content:
RFC 4176 provides a framework for the operation and management of Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks. The framework is meant to produce a coherent description of the significant technical issues that are important in the design of L3VPN management solutions. The selection of specific approaches, and the choices among information models and protocols, are outside the scope of the document.

The terminology matters for the rest of the framework. A VPN is a set of transmission and switching resources that will be used over a shared infrastructure to process the IP traffic that characterizes communication services between the sites or premises interconnected via this VPN. An L3VPN interconnects sets of hosts and routers based on Layer 3 addresses. A VPN instance, from a management standpoint, is the collection of configuration information associated with a specific VPN, residing on a PE router. A VPN site is a VPN customer's location that is connected to the service provider network via a CE-PE link, and which can access at least one VPN. A VPN service provider is a service provider that offers VPN-related services, and a VPN customer is a customer that bought VPNs from one. A customer agent is the entity responsible for requesting VPN customer-specific information.

Two documents carry the promises. A Service Level Agreement is a contractual agreement between the service provider and the customer, which includes qualitative and quantitative metrics that define service quality guarantees and retribution procedures when service levels are not being met. The Service Level Specifications are internally focused service performance specifications, used by the service provider to manage customer service quality levels.

For any type of Layer 3 VPN, having a management platform where the VPN-related information could be collected and managed is recommended. A service and network management system may centralize information related to instances of a VPN and allow users to configure and provision each instance from a central location. A service provider must be able to manage the capabilities and characteristics of its VPN services, and customers should have means to ensure fulfillment of the VPN service to which they subscribed. To the extent possible, automated operations and interoperability with standard management protocols should be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Two documents sit at the heart of the framework. One is the contract with the customer, which says what quality of service is promised and what happens if it is not met. The other is the provider's own internal version of the same promises, used to run the network. Everything else in the memo hangs off those two.

sections.title: The Reference Models
sections.content:
The memo adopts the generic requirements structure of the ITU-T Telecommunications Management Network, which has three layers. At the bottom, engineer, deploy and manage the switching, routing and transmission resources supporting the service, from a network perspective, which is network element management. Above that, manage the VPNs deployed over these resources, which is network management. Above that again, manage the VPN service, which is service management.

Two reference models are given, one for PE-based L3VPN management and one for CE-based L3VPN management. In both, a customer agent sits on the customer side of a customer interface and talks to a service manager, which sits in the service management layer and administrates customer-specific attributes such as the customer identifier, personal information including name, address, phone number and credit card number, subscription services and parameters, access control policy information, and billing and statistical information. The provider network manager sits in the network management layer and talks to the service manager. In the PE-based model, the provider network manager administrates device attributes and their relationships, covering PE devices and other devices that construct the corresponding PE-based VPN. In the CE-based model, it administrates those attributes covering both PE and CE devices that construct the corresponding CE-based VPN. In both models the network element management layer covers the PE device, and the customer network on the other side of the customer interface holds the CE device of the VPN.

The memo notes that network and customer service management systems responsible for managing VPN networks have several challenges, depending on the type of VPN network they are required to manage.
sections.plainLanguage: The model is the familiar three-layer one, with the devices at the bottom, the provider's network above them, and the service the customer buys at the top. What is specific to VPNs is the customer interface that runs down the side: the customer's own agent plugs into the provider's service manager, and the provider's network manager sits behind it.

sections.title: Customer Service Management
sections.content:
The customer management function's goal is to manage the service-based operations such as service ordering, service subscription and activation. It resides in the L3VPN service manager at the service management layer, and consists of defining the L3VPN services offered by the provider, collecting and consolidating the customer's L3VPN service requirements, and performing some reporting for the customer. It is correlated with the network management function at the network management layer for initiating the L3VPN services provisioning and for getting some service reporting.

At the service management layer the information framework is composed of Service Level Agreements and Service Level Specifications. Services are described through the agreement, which is a contractual document between customer and provider; the technical part of the service description is the specification, which groups different kinds of parameters, some more related to the description of the transport of the packets and some to the specification of the service itself. A specification may be defined per access network connection, per VPN, per VPN site, and per VPN route. The provider may define objectives and the measurement intervals using Service Level Objective parameters: quality of service and traffic parameters; availability for the site, VPN or access connection; duration of outage intervals per site, route or VPN; service activation interval, for example the time to turn up a new site; trouble report response time interval; time to repair interval; total incoming and outgoing traffic from a site or a VPN route, or that has transited through the whole VPN; and measurement of non-conforming incoming and outgoing traffic. The provider and the customer may negotiate contractual penalties where the provider does not meet a set of specification performance objectives. Traffic parameters and actions should be defined for incoming and outgoing packets that cross the demarcation between the provider's premises and the customer's, so for example traffic policing functions may be activated at the ingress of the provider's network while traffic shaping capabilities could be activated at the egress.

The customer management functions fall into the five traditional fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security categories. Fault management relies on the manipulation of network layer failure information and reports incidents to impacted customers, based on the VPN service offering to which the customer is subscribed; it includes indication of which customer services are impacted by a failure, incident recording or logs, the frequency of tests, the ability to invoke probes from the customer and the provider, and the ability to uncover faults before the customer notices them. Configuration management must be able to configure L3VPN service parameters with the level of detail the customer is able to specify, according to service templates defined by the provider. A service template contains fields which, when instantiated, yield a definite service requirement or policy: a template for an IPsec tunnel would contain fields such as tunnel end points, authentication modes, encryption and authentication algorithms, shared keys if any, and traffic filters; a BGP and MPLS-based VPN service template would contain the customer premises that need to be interconnected via the VPN; and a quality of service agreement template would contain one-way transit delay, inter-packet delay variation, throughput and packet loss thresholds.

Accounting is provided with network layer measurements information and manages it. The customer manager is responsible for retrieval of accounting information from the provider network manager, and for the analysis, storage and administration of measurements. Some providers may require near-real time reporting of measurement information, and may offer it as part of a customer network management service. If a provider supports a dynamic bandwidth management service, the schedule and the amount of the bandwidth required to perform requested allocation changes must be traceable for monitoring and accounting purposes. Performance management from the customer's perspective includes the determination of the conformance level with the specifications, such as quality of service and availability measurements; the objective is to correlate accounting information with performance and fault management information to produce billing that takes into account the agreement for periods where the objectives are not met. The information should reflect the quality of the subscribed service as perceived by the customer, may be measured by the provider or by a third party, and the parameters used to reflect the performance level could be negotiated and agreed between the provider and the customer during the service negotiation phase. It should also support analysis of bandwidth utilization, response time, availability, quality of service statistics and trends. Security management includes management features to guarantee the security of the VPN: the security of devices, configuration data and access connections, with authentication and authorization, or access control, also in this category.

The customer-facing side is drawn as three functional blocks in the service manager: VPN offering management, which is how the provider advertises the services it offers so that potential customers can select the one they want to subscribe to, with additional features such as the level of quality associated with the delivery of the service, the level of management performed by the provider, and security options; VPN order management, which manages the requests initiated by the customers and tracks the status of the achievement of the related operations, with the activation of orders conditioned by the availability of the resources that meet the customer's requirements with the agreed guarantees; and VPN service assurance, under which the provider should monitor, measure and provide statistical information to the customer, assuming an agreement between both parties on the measurement methodology and on the quality of service indicators. A customer must have a means to view the topology, operational state, order status and other parameters associated with the VPN service offering that has been subscribed. Communication between customer agents and the service provider will rely on a query and response mechanism, and a customer who cannot afford the resources to manage its own customer edge equipment should be able to outsource the management of the VPN to the service provider.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the part of the system the customer sees. It has to offer services, take orders, and then keep checking that what was promised is what is being delivered. The measurements that prove it are the same ones used for billing, which is why the memo says they have to be correlated carefully.

sections.title: The Provider Network Manager
sections.content:
When implementing a VPN architecture within a domain, or a set of domains managed by a single provider, the provider must have a means to view the physical and logical topology of the VPN premises, the VPN operational status, the service ordering status, the service handling, the service activation status, and other aspects associated with each customer's VPN. From the provider's perspective, managing a VPN service consists mainly of managing the customers in terms of the agreement, where the term customer denotes a role rather than the end user, so a provider could itself be a customer; managing the VPN premises, especially creating, modifying and deleting operations, editing the related information for a specific link, or supervising the AAA operations; managing the CE-PE links, particularly creating, modifying and deleting links and editing the related information for a specific VPN; and managing the service ordering, such as quality of service, in terms of supported classes of service and traffic isolation.

The memo argues against proprietary management methods. The additional expense associated with operators having to use multiple proprietary configuration-related management methods, such as command line interface languages, to access such systems is not recommended, because it affects the overall cost of the service, especially when multiple vendor technologies are used. Devices should therefore provide standards-based interfaces, and the additional requirements on possible interoperability issues and availability of standardized management interfaces need to be investigated.

The provider's network management functions again fall into the five categories. Fault management includes fault detection, with incident reports, alarms and failure visualization; fault localization, with analysis of alarm reports and diagnostics; and corrective actions on the data path, routing and resource allocation. Since L3VPNs rely on a common network infrastructure, the provider network manager provides a means to inform the service manager about which VPN customers are impacted by a failure in the infrastructure, and should provide pointers to the related customer configuration information to contribute to fault isolation and the determination of corrective actions. It is desirable to detect faults caused by configuration errors, because these may cause the VPN service to fail or not meet other requirements such as traffic and routing isolation; one approach could be a protocol that systematically checks that all constraints have been taken into account and that consistency checks have been enforced during the tunnel configuration process. A capability for checking IP reachability within a VPN must be provided for diagnostic purposes, as must a capability for checking the configuration of a VPN device.

Configuration management is required in order to deploy VPNs, provisioning at least the following L3VPN components: PE, CE, hierarchical tunnels, access connections, routing and quality of service, and if access to the Internet is provided that option must also be configurable. Provisioning for adding or removing VPN customer premises should be as automated as possible, and the provider network manager must ensure that devices and protocols are provisioned consistently and correctly, providing a means for checking whether a service order is correctly provisioned. Configuration errors can arise from manual configuration, intruder attacks, and conflicting service requirements. The specific requirements are that the manager must support configuration of VPN membership; should use identifiers for providers, L3VPNs, PEs, CEs, hierarchical tunnels and access connections; must configure tunnels between PE and CE devices, which requires coordination of tunnel identifiers, paths, VPNs and any associated service information such as a quality of service service; must configure the routing protocols running between PE routers and CE devices, and for multicast services the multicast routing protocols as well; and must configure the routing protocols running between PE routers, and between PE and P routers.

For a PE-based service, the routing protocols between PE routers and CE devices must be configured on a per-VPN basis, with the manager supporting configuration of a CE routing protocol for each access connection, and the configuration of a PE-based L3VPN should be coordinated with the configuration of the underlying infrastructure, including the Layer 1 and Layer 2 networks that interconnect the components of the VPN. If there is an IGP running within the L3VPN, the manager must provision the related parameters, including metrics, capacity, quality of service capability and restoration parameters. It must provision network access between provider-managed PE and CE equipment. When a security service is requested, the manager must provision the entities and associated parameters involved in the service: for IPsec services, tunnels, options, keys and other parameters should be provisioned at either the CE or the PE routers, and for an intrusion detection service the filtering and detection rules should be provisioned on a VPN basis.

The provider should also have a means to dynamically provision the resources associated with VPN services, for example in a PE-based service the number and size of virtual switching and forwarding table instances. Dynamic VPN resource allocation is crucial to cope with the frequent requests for changes expressed by customers, such as sites joining or leaving a VPN, as well as to achieve scalability, and the PE routers should be able to dynamically assign the VPN resources, which is especially important for dial-up and wireless VPN services. Many providers also offer value-added services such as Internet access, firewall services, intrusion detection, IP telephony and IP Centrex, application hosting and backup, and the VPN service should be able to provide access to these. A VPN service should allow the provider to supply the customer with different kinds of well-known IP services, such as DNS, NTP and RADIUS, needed for ordinary network operation and management, and the provider should be able to provide IP services to multiple customers from one or many servers. A firewall function may be required to restrict access to the L3VPN from the Internet, and managed firewalls may be supported on a per-VPN basis although multiple VPNs will be supported by the same physical device, in which case they should be provided at the access points of the L3VPN. Configuration of interworking L3VPN solutions should also be supported, taking security and end-to-end quality of service issues into account.

Accounting at this level is the measurement of resource utilization. Performance management includes monitoring and collecting performance data regarding devices, facilities and services, and the manager must monitor device behaviour to evaluate performance metrics associated with a specification, using measurement techniques that may be intrusive or non-intrusive depending on the parameters being monitored. It must also monitor aspects of the VPN not directly associated with a specification, such as resource utilization, the status of devices and transmission facilities, and the control of monitoring resources such as probes and remote agents at network access points used by customers and mobile users. Devices supporting L3VPN whose level of quality is defined by specifications should have real-time performance measurements with indicators and threshold crossing alerts, and such thresholds should be configurable. Security management must include management features to guarantee the preservation of the confidentiality of customers' traffic and control data, and the manager must support standard methods for authenticating users attempting to access VPN services.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the provider's side of the same arrangement. It has to build and change the VPNs, watch the shared infrastructure for faults, and work out which customers each fault affects. The memo is firm about automation: adding a site should not mean a person typing commands into three different vendors' routers.

sections.title: L3VPN Devices and Their Management Interfaces
sections.content:
Each L3VPN solution must specify the management information, in the form of MIBs, PIBs or XML schemas, for the network elements involved in L3VPN services. The memo calls this an essential requirement in network provisioning. The approach should identify any L3VPN-specific information not contained in a standards track MIB module.

The deployment of a VPN may span a wide range of network equipment, potentially including equipment from multiple vendors. The provisioning of a unified network management view of the VPN shall therefore be simplified by means of standard management interfaces and models. This will also facilitate customer self-managed, that is self-monitored, network devices or systems.

Where significant configuration is required whenever a new service is to be provisioned, it is important, for scalability reasons, that the network management system provides a largely automated mechanism for the relevant configuration operations. Manual configuration of VPN services, for new sites or for re-provisioning existing ones, could lead to scalability issues and should be avoided. It is thus important for network operators to maintain visibility of the complete picture of the VPN through the management system, and this should be achieved by using standards track protocols such as SNMP. The use of proprietary command-line interfaces is not recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The devices themselves have to be describable to a management system, and the same description has to work across vendors. Otherwise every new customer means someone typing at a console, and the provider cannot grow.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says that although it discusses and addresses some security concerns in its sections on customer and provider security management, it does not introduce any new security concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here creates a new risk. The security work is the access control and authentication described earlier, which are part of the management functions rather than a separate addition.

viz.caption: THE THREE MANAGEMENT LAYERS OF THE REFERENCE MODEL

layers.label: Service management layer
layers.detail: The service manager, which administrates customer-specific attributes such as the customer identifier, subscription parameters, access control policy and billing information

layers.label: Network management layer
layers.detail: The provider network manager, which plans, builds, provisions and maintains the network resources to meet the service level agreements

layers.label: Network element management layer
layers.detail: Engineer, deploy and manage the switching, routing and transmission resources supporting the service

items.title: Fault management
items.text: Reports incidents to impacted customers, based on the service offering they are subscribed to. Includes recording logs, the frequency of tests, the ability to invoke probes, and uncovering faults before the customer notices them.

items.title: Configuration management
items.text: Configures service parameters to the level of detail the customer can specify, using service templates defined by the provider.

items.title: Accounting
items.text: Retrieves accounting information from the provider network manager, and analyses, stores and administers the measurements.

items.title: Performance management
items.text: Determines the conformance level with the service level specifications, correlating accounting, performance and fault information to produce billing.

items.title: Security management
items.text: Guarantees the security of the VPN: the security of devices, configuration data and access connections, including authentication and access control.

items.title: Fault management
items.text: Fault detection through incident reports, alarms and failure visualization; fault localization through analysis and diagnostics; and corrective actions on the data path, routing and resource allocation.

items.title: Configuration management
items.text: Provisions PE, CE, hierarchical tunnels, access connections, routing and quality of service, and coordinates the tunnels and the underlying infrastructure.

items.title: Performance management
items.text: Monitors device behaviour to evaluate performance metrics against the specifications, and monitors resource utilization, device status and transmission facilities.

items.title: Security management
items.text: Guarantees the preservation of the confidentiality of customers' traffic and control data, and supports standard methods for authenticating users.
